The 36 Best Gifts for Dads (2026)

📅 Dec 17, 2025  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

It occurs to me that, as a new(ish) father, and someone who reviews products for a living, I am a nightmare to get gifts for. I’m not alone. Most of my friends have no idea what to get their dad, and end up brainstorming in group chats with anyone they can get their hands on.

Fear not, I’m here to make gifting a little easier this year (or at the very least, contribute to the brainstorm). Below are some of the best WIRED-tested gifts for the dad or father figure in your life, including travel gadgets, dad-approved apparel, and best-in-class earbuds. I’ve personally gifted a few of these to my dad, with great results.

Updated September 2026: I completely overhauled this guide with 27 new picks, including tech accessories, headphones, dad-approved apparel, fitness gear, and more.

This is my favorite power bank, full stop. If I am traveling, going abroad, camping, or just headed to work, I take this power bank. It’s the built-in, retractable USB-C cord that does it for me—it’s there when you need it, and out of the way when you don’t. It’s small enough to pack in any bag and light enough that I barely notice it. Plus, it has an extra USB-A and USB-C port built in, so you can charge multiple devices at once if you want.

I’ve lost count of how many times my Apple AirTag Bluetooth tracker has saved me from the hassle of looking for something. Keys: located. Luggage: tracked. Backpack: safe and sound. Sure, it’s not the most exciting gift in the world, but it’s the epitome of useful and practical. As long as they use an iPhone, that is.

“If you told me I could only have one bag in my life, the 26L version of the GoRuck GR1 would be my pick,” says WIRED operations manager and outdoor expert Scott Gilbertson (he’s also a dad). It’s absolutely in buy-it-for-life territory, built with ultra-durable, water-resistant 1000D Cordura and tested by US Army Special Forces. It’s technically made for rucking, but it can do basically anything you throw at it, travel included. This Huckberry version omits the exterior MOLLE webbing, giving it a sleeker look. You can read more in Gilbertson’s full GoRuck GR1 review.

The best aluminum carry-on suitcase. Aluminum luggage is sleek and durable, with a shell that just looks better with little dents and dings (unlike polycarbonate luggage). Aluminum itself is recyclable and repairable, and the clamps that hold the Rimowa together won’t fail or break as easily as your typical zipper. Rimowa is obviously the “it” brand for this type of luggage, but you can get similar options from Away and Level8 for well under half the price.

A reusable water bottle is something I thought I only needed one of. Turns out, the more the merrier. I now have four and have realized there’s a good place for each one (in my case, one for the house, one for my work bag, and one for the nightstand). The Owala FreeSip has been my favorite for years, usurping my Hydro Flask and S’well for water bottle supremacy. Plus it comes in literally dozens of colors—there’s definitely one he’ll love.

I’ve become a camera person since becoming a dad, with a growing collection that’s frankly getting a little out of hand. Camp Snap is part of that camera pile. It’s one of the simplest ways to take pictures without getting distracted by your phone or overwhelmed by mirrorless camera settings to fiddle with. This latest model adds desperately needed updates like a button to toggle between filters and a faster shutter button. It also comes in a bunch of fun colors, including a few transparent options that remind me of my old Game Boy Color.

Look: The Amazon Kindle Scribe is a perfectly good digital notebook. But the Montblanc Digital Paper has one of the best digital pens money can buy. (It makes sense: The brand is known for its pens, after all.) This luxury E Ink tablet has a slim metal aluminum frame, leather side panel, and superb writing feel. The pen itself comes with three interchangeable tips that change the writing feel and resistance.

If Dad loves to host large get-togethers, parties, or tailgates, this portable party speaker is one of the loudest, most durable I’ve tested. It’s got a clean, understated, loudspeaker-slash-rock-concert look that’s a far cry from the light-show techno vibes of most portable party speakers. It’s very durable, with large silicone balls on each corner for impact protection. Plus, it has a swappable battery. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised if it outlasts most other speakers in his collection. You can learn more in my full Soundboks Rider review.

If he owns an iPhone, chances are he would appreciate an upgraded pair of wireless earbuds. I’ve been testing the newest Apple AirPods 5 for a few weeks now, and I’ve been truly impressed with how good the noise-canceling is, especially for earbuds without eartips. The version I linked above also has improved battery life, a wireless charging case, and volume-swipe controls on each earbud stem.

The classic business traveler over-ear headphones. I’ve been testing these latest Bose for nearly a month now, and they are some of the most comfortable over-ear headphones you can get, with dang good noise-canceling too. If Dad loves his music, podcasts, and TV shows, no matter where he is, these will be a trusty companion for his next adventure, whether that’s on the couch or on his next long-haul flight.

Teenage Engineering needs little introduction—the Swedish company makes some of the nicest-looking, nicest-feeling gadgets that are the envy of basically everyone who doesn’t own one. This is one of the brand's portable samplers, sequencers, and composers that Dad can make music on, wherever he is. Despite its small size, it has ample pads and dials, a built-in microphone and line input for audio recording, 64GB of internal memory, and 999 sample slots.

My vinyl era started long before I became a dad, but it’s only since then that I started caring about how a turntable looks. This one from Flaunce is a minimal faux wood model that looks elegant on a shelf or table, but lets the vinyl take center stage. It has an upgradable cartridge and a built-in phono preamp—Dad just needs to plug it into some powered bookshelf speakers, and voilà.

I basically lived in one of these tees during parental leave. It’s absolutely the softest tee I own, with a fabric that never bothered my sensitive skin. It’s athletic without being too slim-fitting, stretchy without feeling cheap, and a great do-everything (or do nothing on the couch) tee for anyone, not just Dad.

Another do-everything piece of apparel, but decidedly more technical than the Vuori tee. These are my go-to pants for walks, hikes, and camping trips. They are very lightweight and have a reasonably athletic fit, water-repellent finish, adjustable drawstring waist, and durable ripstop polyester I’ve yet to poke a hole through.

The gift that never fails. I’ve seen the Brooks Ghost gifted to me, my dad, my father-in-law, and others. No one has ever looked disappointed. These are great running shoes for just about anyone, with neutral support and plenty of cushion. I’ve used the 18s (and previous 17s, 16s, 15s) for dozens of miles of walking and running this year—they are comfortable and reliable. Plus, you are supposed to replace your running shoes every six months or so, which I’m sure your dad has not done.

Dads who run need more running shirts. I certainly do. This Ten Thousand Session Shirt is one of my go-tos because it is breathable enough for a serious run, but looks normal enough to go to the cafe afterward. It’s made from 100 percent polyester—no nylon or spandex to be found here, which means it dries fast and absorbs very little water, in my experience.

Sneakers in the office are going extinct—haven’t you heard? WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman noticed these on GQ editor Jordan Bowman, and we have to pass along his personal recommendation because the “buttery smooth” leather alone is worth a small splurge. This style has a mercifully wider toe box than most loafers tried, and they’re versatile enough to complement both Levi’s and formal slacks. They’re the platonic ideal of office footwear.

WIRED senior innovation editor and resident watch expert Jeremy White is very into this new Speedmaster collection, going so far as to call them “mini Moonwatches.” (The Omega Moonwatch is kind of a big deal.) That’s because the revamped collection has rounded subdials and overhauled bezels, like those on the—you guessed it—Moonwatch. Either way, it’s an iconic, timeless watch built to last, and it comes in 11 styles.

I can’t think of many dads who don’t love an electric bike. The Letric XP4 750 isn’t just one of WIRED’s top electric bike picks, it’s one of the best-selling electric vehicles in America, ranking third behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 in 2024. WIRED reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani says it only took 20 minutes to assemble and lasted well over 50 miles of riding on a single charge. This version has an upgraded 750-watt motor that helps tackle hillier terrain than the original.

A headlamp is an infinitely useful outdoor tool—you can use it for camping; yard work (early or late in the day); home maintenance; or, if you’re my dad, grilling after the sun has set. I’ve loved using this Biolite headlamp in 2026. It’s bright, comfortable, and has multiple modes, including a focused beam mode, wide floodlight mode, and red-light mode that I’ve loved for bikepacking. Plus it’s USB-C rechargeable—no more rummaging through the battery drawer for AAs.

This premium cooler is the gift that will last them for years and years. It’s made with double-walled vacuum insulation, just like a travel mug. In practice, that means it can keep things cool with less than half as much ice as a regular cooler, and has much thinner walls, which makes for a larger interior space. Yes, it’s pricier than a regular cooler, but its premium design, lightweight body, and ultra-efficient cooling make it a winner for dads everywhere.

I will readily admit I am not a knife guy, but I love this knife. I’m not alone—it’s featured in our Buy It for Life guide, and comes recommended by me, former WIRED senior director Martin Cizmar, and over 2,000 five-star reviews on Amazon. Sure, it’s probably not as bulletproof as that matte-black EDC high-end pocket knife that costs $300, but it’s timeless, classy, and elegant.

If he loves ultralight, this is the cup for him. If he has no idea what ultralight is but wants a super lightweight cup for drinks or snacks around the house, this too is a fun option. Snow Peak is one of our favorite outdoor gear brands, and its lightweight titanium cookware is some of its most popular. I’ve used this cup on bikepacking trips and for snacking around the house alike.

I didn’t think I needed a tiny portable vacuum (I have a perfectly good cordless vacuum), but I was gifted this tiny Hoto vacuum years ago, and it has been endlessly useful. I use it to clean strollers, keyboards, my desk, you name it. It’s small and portable enough to take anywhere you need a quick clean. I gifted one to my brother-in-law, and he uses it to clean his car constantly—it basically lives in his car’s glove compartment.

An on-board diagnostic scanner plugs into your car’s port and pairs to your phone via Bluetooth so you can read and troubleshoot your car’s error codes. It’s a great way for tinkerers to fix car issues themselves and avoid a time-consuming trip to the shop. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar recommended this scanner from BlueDriver. It has a lot of powerful features that don’t require any subscription to use (unlike many competitors).

Noco makes some of the best portable jump starters—emphasis on portable. This battery-powered jump starter charges with a regular USB-C cable, and is a must-have for anyone who wants to avoid waiting for a buddy car or waiting for a tow. WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage tested all kinds of jump starters on his old Land Cruiser, and recommends this one as the best compact option. Not only can it start your car, it can recharge your phone, just like a regular power bank would.

This is the best pizza oven for the dad who doesn’t have space for a full-sized outdoor one. It’s an indoor electric pizza oven that can fit on a countertop, and can heat to up to 850 degrees Fahrenheit. Like all of the brand’s appliances, it’s easy to use, so it's more fun than work to make that fan-favorite pizza just right.

When my son was born last year, I lost the time to grind and brew, so I found myself stocking my fridge with disappointingly bitter bulk-bottled iced coffee (or spending $7 on a café cold brew). My wife got us a coffee subscription to Cometeer, which flash-freezes freshly ground small-batch coffee and ships them in recyclable pods—just add water, hot or cold, to dial in the strength. You can take the time to mix and match roasters each month or just set your faves and forget it. After six months of testing, I can safely say I haven’t had a bad cup. I miss the aromatics I get and comfort I feel from a truly fresh grind, but each pour feels like a tiny treat, even at 5 am. It’s a whole little moment: My 16-month-old chugs his bottle while I stir up oat milk, ice, and Counter Culture. He’s learning to say “cheers.” I look forward to those early mornings a bit more than I used to. —Cooper Fleishman

If they love a cocktail, this toolkit from Umami Mart elevates the mixing experience to something more refined. Umami Mart is an independently owned small business in Oakland that’s part sake bar, part sake class space, and part online barware store. This kit includes a diamond-cut mixing glass, julep strainer, stainless steel jigger, and stainless steel teardrop barspoon, all made in Japan and sourced by the brand.

The Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

Tossing a Frisbee around is part fun: part an excuse to hang out and talk. It’s a classic dads-and-kids activity that lasts for years, even as interests and hobbies change. Former WIRED director Martin Cizmar says that, over time, the ask to toss the Frisbee around shifts from the kid to the adult. Either way, the Aerobie is one of the best flying discs you can buy.

Perhaps the best water gun ever made, the SpryaFour is a very powerful squirt gun that can shoot accurately from up to 50 feet away. It has a fully digital smart display that lets you select between shooting styles and shows you how much ammo you have left. It refills much faster than the SpyraThree (20 shots in about 12 seconds). It’s recommended for kids (and adults) 14 and up.

These are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. That’s why I love them for outdoor runs and bike rides. This premium model uses a mix of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that’s clearer than most smaller open earbuds. You can learn more in our full Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 review.

Another classic gift I’ve seen win over not just dad, but everyone else in the room, too (everyone wanted a turn). This massage gun has the signature Theragun triangle grip, which makes it far easier to target hard to reach places compared to other brands that have a straight grip. It comes with three ball head attachments (standard, dampener, and thumb), and lasts up to 120 minutes on a single charge.

This Garmin watch is just right for the dad who is getting really into running and wants to dig into more advanced metrics and detailed training plans than what’s offered on most smartwatches. Like any good fitness tracker, the Forerunner 165 has superb battery life (up to 11 days), a colorful touchscreen, and plenty of buttons that make it easy to control with gloved or sweaty hands. It’s also one of the brand’s most affordable running watches. You can learn more in our full Garmin Forerunner 165 review.

The Best Made-in-USA Gifts for Every Person on Your Shopping List

📅 Nov 24, 2025  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

From trusted tools to road-trip essentials, we rounded up the toughest gear made in the United States for the car people in your life.

This article was updated in November 2026 with new products and information.

There’s a particular satisfaction in picking up a tool or piece of gear and knowing where it was made. It’s more than patriotism: a pair of boots stitched in Michigan or a kitchen tool forged in Ohio carries a connection to the people and skills behind it.

Buying American-made products helps support the craftspeople, businesses, and communities that keep making things here. And finding those products doesn’t have to be a treasure hunt. We’ve rounded up standout U.S.-made picks for weekend wrenchers, road-trip warriors, and everyone in between.

The brass bolsters and wood handle give the iconic Buck Knives 110 Folding Hunter Knife a significant heft that exudes quality. Made in Post Falls, Idaho, it locks open with a satisfying click and holds an edge through serious cutting tasks. It is not the most high-tech blade on the market, but it is a timeless tool that feels great in the hand.

Most carry-on bags feel flimsy, but the Pelican ATX 22 feels like you could drag it behind the car on the highway and it would survive. Hell, I'm not even sure a particularly grumpy baggage handler could destroy this thing.

The layout is simple, but the injection-molded construction is undeniably Pelican. This particular model is sized just right to fit in the overhead bin without a fight, and you can rest assured clothes and gear will be protected from the elements better than standard fabric luggage ever could manage.

Built just down the road from me in Rockford, Michigan, these Wolverine 1000 Mile Boots are no joke. While they do require a significant break-in period, the payoff is worth the blister or two.

Once the Horween leather molds to your foot, these boots feel like a second skin that look as good as they feel and are tough enough for daily wear. The Goodyear welt construction also means you can resole them in a few years rather than tossing them in the trash when the tread wears down.

As you'd expect from a brand as synonymous with quality as Channellock, this Tool Roll-5 is the kind of pliers kit that just works, day in and day out. The cutters bite cleanly, the tongue-and-groove jaws actually meet, and the pivots don't wobble after a season of real use.

The included roll keeps everything from clanking around in the trunk or bottoming out in a drawer and is great for keeping forgetful DIYers such as myself from losing them in the middle of projects. As all products on this list, these tools are made in the USA and tough enough to hand to a neighbor without worrying about getting them back bent.

Manufactured in the US, the Smithey 5.5-quart dutch oven skips the fragile enamel coatings found on expensive European imports in favor of bare, heavily seasoned cast iron. You can drag it across steel grill grates or bury it directly in glowing campfire coals without worrying about chipping a delicate finish. And it works equally well atop gas, electric, and induction stovetops.

The sheer mass of the walls and dome lid acts like a thermal battery, locking in steady, even heat for hours to properly break down tough cuts of meat and soften even the most stubborn carrots. It’s a heavy-duty, straightforward piece of American hardware that handles campfire stews and kitchen braises with equal capability.

If you're looking to pair the Dutch oven with a skillet, or simply don't need the massive capacity of a 5.5-quart pot, the Smithey No. 10 is the logical alternative. Like the rest of their South Carolina-forged lineup, it features a machined, glass-smooth interior that eliminates the stubborn break-in period typical of modern cast iron. It cooks with the non-stick capability of a well-worn vintage piece right out of the box.

The 10-inch diameter hits the sweet spot for daily duty, whether you're searing a pair of ribeyes over an open fire or frying eggs on a kitchen stove, although there are plenty of other sizes available on Smithey's website if you're hoping to go smaller or larger. I'd also recommend picking up a chainmail scrubber to get out the more stubborn food remnants, and Smithey's salt keeper is an adorable accessory to boot.

Having a heavy-duty piece of American metal that takes high heat without warping, wipes clean in seconds, and feels substantial enough to outlast your vehicle fundamentally changes how you operate in the kitchen.

The GoRuck GR1 is overkill for a commute, which is exactly why you will like it. Made in America by a veteran-owned company, this bag has straps that are padded perfectly to handle heavy loads, and the laptop compartment is suspended to protect your tech from drops. It opens flat for easy packing and shrugs off rain and abrasions like they are nothing.

I've personally owned one of these for more than 15 years now, and it's been everything from a daily backpack in college to a tool bag that's been used and abused during car repairs. While the 1000D Cordura is certainly faded and the zipper pulls have been replaced a few times, it still performs just as it did on day one.

Finding quality local products oftentimes requires giving up a Saturday morning. You have to navigate a farmer's market, walk the stalls, and sift through the inventory to find something worthwhile. The Farmers Finds outsources that legwork by scouring regional markets across the country, buying small-batch goods from independent makers, and packing them into a single box. It’s a straightforward logistical solution akin to a regional community supported agriculture (CSA) box. Instead of driving across state lines to find a specific local preserve or hot sauce, it arrives directly on your porch.You can order a single box, though the subscription model is how the service is really meant to be used. The monthly tier delivers two to four items from a single brand, while the quarterly option scales up to seven to ten products sourced from five different makers. It's a practical gift for someone who appreciates regional goods, but doesn't have the bandwidth to track down the vendors themselves. You get quality American-made products, and the makers get the business.

What more can I say about Duck Tape Duct Tape that hasn't already been said? Sure, it's never a long-term solution to automotive or home problems, but it'll get the job done until you find a more permanent solution. Hopefully you'll never have to use it, but for 10 bucks or so, it's nice insurance to throw in the trunk for the inevitable emergency.

The Wave is one of Leatherman's most iconic tools, and while it takes on a new shape with the Wave Alpha, it's still the answer when you want one thing that handles 10 small jobs and you don't feel like going back to the toolbox.

This all-in-one tool features one-hand blades, real pliers, actual drivers, a large scissor tool, and more. Leatherman backs it with a no-drama warranty, and their stuff is easy to service if you get it gritty (I've sent in my original Wave for service twice and had it back within a week with little more than the shipping cost to send it out).

Odds are this tool will outlast whoever you give it to, so consider it a long-term investment made right here in the United States.

If you want deep color and gloss for a weekend cruiser, this Griot's Garage Best of Show Wax gets the job done. Formulated just west of Indianapolis, Indiana, it goes on smooth and buffs off without leaving stubborn white dust in the panel gaps.

While it's easy enough to use with a hand buff, it works equally well with an electric buffer if you want to expedite the process. It's affordable, it works well, and overall it delivers a robust shine with a little bit of elbow grease.

Duke Cannon's Big Ass Brick of Soap is comically big at first, but then you realize it outlasts three normal ones and doesn't turn into goo in the shower. I've purchased and used a dozen of these over the last decade, and every time I go through a single bar, my spouse has already gone through a three-pack of normal ones.

The scent of this particular bar (they have dozens of scents/formulations to choose from) is more warm "vanilla/wood" than "spill at the distillery," but it does have that signature bourbon smell you'd expect from a little Buffalo Trace.

This Rite in the Rain notepad lets you write down torque values, weird part numbers, or your "What's that noise?" notes, all without having to worry about whether the pages will smear if your hands are greasy or it's misting outside.

The covers hold up in a pocket, and the wire doesn't explode into a tangle like some other cheap pads I've used over the years. It's a bit pricey for a small notepad, but when you need a reliable notepad that can take on the elements and solvents, you won't find a better option.

As a Michigander, I'm a bit biased, but Carhartt Beanies are just a way of life (second only to Stormy Kromers). While not all versions are made in America, there are Woodside Beanies made right here in the States. Just be sure to check the product listing to confirm before making your purchase.

This American-made bag takes a beating and looks all the better for it. The rugged twill of the Filson Original Briefcase resists water and wear, while the bridle leather handles soften up nicely over time. It is heavy for what it holds, but it protects a laptop and documents with a style that works as well in a truck as it does in an office.

LED technology revived the classic Maglite form factor you remember from your childhood. Built in Ontario, California, it still has the heft that feels reassuring in your hand, but now it throws a beam that properly lights up the road ahead (or engine beneath you). You get a simple focus twist mechanism, as well as the convenience of D-cell batteries that are easy enough to find at any gas station.

Smell like you upgraded to a nicer car. Drift infuses a magnetized wood block with clean-ingredient essential oils—teak, amber, and cedar—then snaps it to a low-profile metal visor clip. It's made in the U.S., looks grown-up, and takes quick monthly refill blocks when the scent fades. No dangling trees, no headaches.

Pouring fluids into a cramped engine bay usually results in a mess, but this FlexAll Flexible Funnel by TEC Products solves that geometry problem.

The nitrile rubber handles oil and gas without degrading, and you can mold it around hoses and wires to create a leak-free path. Sure, it might be a bit more of a hassle to clean when you're done, but the convenience of the gooseneck makes all the difference when trying to get fluids into all the nooks and crannies of modern vehicles.

The lifetime warranty is real, but the comfort is why you will keep buying them. Knit in Northfield, Vermont, these Darn Tough Micro Crew Socks breathe well inside a driving shoe or a heavy boot, and the merino wool blend doesn't stink after a long day on the road.

You will have a hard time wearing a hole in a pair, which makes the higher price tag feel like a bargain over the long haul. I've had probably a dozen pair of Darn Tough socks over the years, and I only managed to wear a hole in one, which was only thanks to a little nail sticking out of my home's mid-century wood floors. And, of course, Darn Tough promptly replaced it with a brand-new pair.

You usually buy emergency kits hoping you wasted your money, because nobody wants to have to use one. But when you get stranded on a dark shoulder, this Pelican SRVL2 2-Person Emergency Kit is exactly what you want to have in the cargo area.

Made and assembled in Torrance, California, this kit organizes the chaos of emergency prep (water pouches, food rations, and first-aid gear) into a distinct, bombproof case that protects the contents from moisture or being crushed. You can toss it in the trunk and forget about it until the moment you really need it.

The integrated handles and wheels are great for easy transfer between cars or garages and the neatly organized bags, and instructions inside all but ensure you'll be better prepared than anyone in the neighborhood if you ever do end up needing it.

According to the FTC, a product must be “all or virtually all” made in the United States. That means final assembly and significant processing happen in the USA, and nearly all components are made and sourced in the USA.

No. “Assembled in the USA” means the product was put together in the USA, but some parts may come from other countries.

Look for the product’s country-of-origin information and check the manufacturer’s website for details about where it is made, assembled, and sourced.

There are a lot of reasons why, but mainly because shopping U.S.-made goods means you are supporting domestic manufacturers, workers, supply chains.

The Best Recipes to Bring to a Potluck, According to Eater Editors

📅 Nov 16, 2025  |  Category: World  |  Read Source →

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a big party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

This is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

Dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with big flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit

I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining

Back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Experts on How to Brighten Under Eyes

📅 Nov 14, 2025  |  Category: Lifestyle  |  Read Source →

Without fail, the eyes are usually the first place a busy week (or month) shows up. A late night, skipping your skin-care routine, or long flight easily translates to a little puffiness in the morning or some shadowing underneath, and maybe even the dreaded “eye bag.” It happens to everyone, and it usually fades once you’ve caught up on sleep, gotten back on your regimen, and have hydrated enough.

Some of it comes down to how the area is built. The skin around the eyes is thinner than on the rest of the face, so whatever’s going on underneath, like fluid that settled overnight or tiny blood vessels close to the surface, is easier to see. Over time, collagen gradually decreases and the brows can sit a touch lower, which is a completely normal part of getting older. Still, it’s nice to have a few tricks for the days you want to look as awake as you feel.

The good news? There are plenty of ways we can brighten, lift, and hydrate this area of the face. Some are as easy as curling your lashes or keeping a couple of spoons in the freezer. Other methods, like an eye cream with studied ingredients, work slowly over a few months after a little consistency. If you want to go further, in-office treatments can subtly lift the brow or soften dark circles. Below, our experts share their best tips for brightening and lifting the eye area, starting with the simplest.

Makeup artist Lynsey Alexander has transformed many a tired eye in her time, having worked with models backstage at fashion shows and on shoots for years. She always begins with good eye drops. “I then use a beige pencil secretly inside the eyes–it needs to be a skin-toned color, white is too stark,” she says. “My favorite is from Paris Berlin as it’s quite dry and not overly creamy, something you don’t want as it moves too easily.”

“Dark circles are a common complaint in my office,” says aesthetic doctor, Maryam Zamani, MD. “One of the most common reasons for dark circles is loss of volume in the periorbital area. As we age, the eyelid-cheek junction becomes elongated, and where this junction was once confluent in youth, it becomes demarcated, giving the appearance of dark lower eyelids or tear troughs.” It’s a common problem that can begin from as early as your twenties, and is made worse as collagen stores deplete. Dr Zamani often treats it with “meticulously placed micro-droplets of hyaluronic acid” to restore the lost volume and hydrate. You will see brighter, more awake eyes immediately.

Celebrity makeup artist Mary Philips has prepped clients like Hailey Bieber and Kendall Jenner for years, and she knows tired eyes are usually the first thing to give a face away. Her fix starts with a step she has coined called underglazing. “The under-eye area is one of the first places I focus on when prepping the skin because it’s so delicate, and can show dryness and fine lines more easily,” she says. “‘Underglazing’ is really about giving that area the hydration it needs before applying any makeup. I love using lightweight, hydrating skincare and gently pressing it into the skin to help everything absorb. The goal is to make the skin look naturally plump and hydrated, so you need less makeup to begin with.”

The new wave of the best eye creams are more effective than ever before, and come loaded with efficacious active ingredients to illuminate the area and soften fine lines, while maintaining the integrity of the skin barrier. “Tretinoin has the best evidence behind it–with continued use (for about a year), you see increased cell turnover; cue brightening of the skin and a reduction in wrinkles,” explains dermatologist Emma Craythorne, MD. “Azelaic acid is also brilliant at brightening, if used in strength at five per cent.”

If your issue is puffiness, take care to ensure you opt for a detoxifying eye cream instead of a hydrating formula–according to Dr. Zamani, hydrating eye creams (particularly those with hyaluronic acid) may exacerbate it.

Yes, it’s boring, but what you eat and drink does make a big difference to the eye area. Those who have ever woken up the morning after with eyes that feel like lead will know that. “Keeping salt and alcohol low in your diet is key,” says Dr, Zamani. “And sleeping with a pillow and eye mask can also help.”

To stimulate the area and help de-puff, facialist Nichola Joss recommends gently massaging an eye cream or gel around the outer orbital bone. “You can also use cold teaspoons to gently stimulate, de-puff, improve lymph drainage and brighten the area,” she says. For those more serious about texture and pigmentation, she also recommends the Lyma Laser, which can be used at home.

Turns out there are a lot of veins and capillaries underneath delicate, thin skin in the eye area, which can cause the dark hue we recognize as dark circles. “We can use sophisticated lasers to target the vascular plexus in the upper and lower eyelid,” says aesthetic surgeon, Costas Papageorgiou, MD, who works from Harrods Wellness Clinic in London. “This plexus tends to become more prominent with age as a result of accumulative inflammation and loss of elasticity, to name two.” By addressing (and softening) this area, you can reinstate skin clarity and light reflection–plus it works particularly well when combined with under eye filler.

To address cool tones and general darkness in the area, try color correcting. “For blue undertones, opt for a peach-based concealer,” advises Dr. Alexander, who also adds a touch of YSL’s cult Touche Eclat to reflect light in the area. “Then, set the under eyes with a brightening powder, such as Laura Mercier’s Secret Brightening Powder, for added radiance.”

Simple but effective, curling your eyelashes has an immediate refreshing effect. “Creating a bright, lifted eye is about creating space between the brow and lash line, and drawing attention outwards and upwards,” explains Anna Payne, UK Chanel makeup artist. For a little extra oomph, she suggests applying a dot of highlighting shadow on the centre of the eyelid and inner corner of the eye to create an illuminating spotlight effect.

When we analyze drooping or lacklustre eyes, we don’t often consider that part of the problem might be coming from the forehead. “One of the biggest reasons that the eye area looks tired is that on top of the tiny repetitive blinking movements our eyes have to do each day, we also express an array of emotions through them, too,” says Ada Ooi, TCM practitioner and founder of 001 Skincare. “A lot of our eye movements, such as frowning or surprise, come from muscles in the forehead.” She recommends using a gua sha tool to alleviate the tension built in the frontalis muscles (the vertical muscles that lift the brows). Try cross-friction massage (horizontally, in this case) to break them from their usual position, and release fascia stress.

“Freshly threaded brows have transformational powers,” sys Vanita Parti MBE, founder of Blink Brow Bar. “By de-fluffing, removing excess stragglers and creating two neat, symmetrical brows, you open up the eyes immediately.” Lifting the arch also lifts and sculpts the entire face, so post-thread, seek to define them with a brow pencil or pomade.

If curling your lashes is already part of your morning, think of this as the version that lasts. Lash lift technician and founder of beauty studio Studio.Lbb recommends it to anyone who’d rather skip the curler altogether. “A lash lift enhances your natural lashes by lifting, curling and tinting them for a longer, darker and more defined look—without extensions or mascara,” she says. Results usually last six to eight weeks, so it’s a smart one to book before a vacation or a stretch of early mornings.

For a quick lift without needles, celebrity facialist and founder of M.A.S.C. Studio Alessandro Cirino points to microcurrent, which sends low-level electrical currents through the skin to wake up the muscles underneath. “Microcurrent can help tone and firm the eye contour, for a fresher-looking result,” he adds. As for a permanent result, Cirino says the research is still limited. Think of it more as a refresh before a big day unless you keep up with a daily routine.

Most people think of crow’s feet when it comes to injectables around the eyes, but the brow is the less obvious spot for injection. “When strategically placed, neuromodulators can subtly elevate the outer brow by relaxing the muscles responsible for pulling it downward,” says Dr. Casey Goodman, medical director of TIEV. “In the right patient, even a slight elevation can make the eyes appear more open, rested, and refreshed.” Dosing matters more here than almost anywhere else on the face. “Overcorrecting can compromise natural expression or even create heaviness where we intended to create lift,” Goodman says. “The goal isn’t to make someone look treated. It’s to make them look like themselves, without the subtle signs of fatigue that may not reflect how they actually feel.”

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue's vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry's standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to brightening and lifting treatments, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: modality, ingredients, texture, packaging, finish, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you. Read more about our testing methodology here.

Propane vs. Gas Generators: Pros and Cons

📅 Sep 30, 2025  |  Category: Other  |  Read Source →

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Updated Nov 16, 2026 12:37 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Power outages are a common problem during thunderstorms, so it’s a good idea to have a backup plan ready to go when the lights go out. Gas and propane generators are common choices for home backup power, RV use, and camping trips.

Propane generators, for example, burn cleaner than gasoline generators, but tend to be more costly to purchase and operate. Gasoline generators are more efficient, but the fuel has a shorter shelf life and may not always be available in emergencies due to panic buying at local gas stations. This guide outlines other differences between the two that will help you decide which type of generator is right for your home.

Having a basic understanding of how the different types of generators work can help decide on the right choice for your home. A propane generator operates by burning the propane in an internal combustion engine. This process creates mechanical energy, which is used to turn a rotor within a magnetic field to generate electricity that can then be used to power appliances and other electronic devices.

Choosing a propane emergency generator for the home makes it easier to stockpile fuel for emergencies. Ken Goodrich, Founder and CEO of Kenerator, says “Propane is a great option for home backup power because it stores well and burns clean. Even when natural gas is temporarily shut off due to a natural disaster or infrastructure damage, a propane tank will continue to supply power.” Additionally, propane burns cleaner than gasoline, so you can expect the best propane generators to require less maintenance and produce fewer emissions.

Understanding how much propane a generator uses is key to deciding on the right model for your home, since propane generators tend to have lower fuel efficiency than gasoline generators. “Additionally, propane suppliers usually deliver to customers on a routine basis, so the homeowner needs to ensure they have enough propane to make it through an average outage,” notes Goodrich. It should also be mentioned that propane generators typically cost more up front and have higher operating costs, so they may not be the best choice for those looking for a cheap solution.

Whether you are looking to purchase a gas or propane generator, it’s good to know how the appliance operates. Generally, the operation of a gasoline generator can be described as a process that converts chemical energy into mechanical energy, which in turn produces electrical energy. More specifically, the engine burns gasoline to spin a shaft, which rotates magnets or electromagnetic fields near the stator, a stationary coil of wires. This induces a change in the magnetic field, creating an electrical current in the coils, that can then be used to power connected appliances and electrical devices.

The main benefit of a gas generator is that these appliances are more affordable to purchase and operate than propane generators, though there can be some fluctuation in the energy efficiency between specific models, so don’t hesitate to ask how much gas does a generator use when researching potential products.

Goodrich mentions that “portable gasoline generators are good options for camping and construction sites,” so you can make use of your generator even when you aren’t at home. Goodrich goes on to say that “gasoline generators are affordable, portable, easy to find, and simple to use,” making them a great choice for just about any home.

While gasoline generators may be cheaper to purchase and operate, gas does not burn as cleanly as propane, so there is a higher risk that these appliances will break down or require frequent maintenance to keep them in good condition. “Gasoline engines use carburetors, as opposed to mixers, which clog easily if not run on a weekly or monthly schedule,” Goodrich points out.

If you like the potential of both propane and gasoline generators, but can’t decide between one or the other, then you may find the best dual-fuel generators to be a good alternative. These generators work by switching between gasoline and propane using a manual or automatic fuel selector.

While the engine has the same combustion cycle for both fuels, it utilizes a built-in carburetor to atomize gasoline for combustion, but when using propane, the fuel passes through a separate external line and regulator before it is pulled into the engine by the vacuum created by the piston. Goodrich says that dual-fuel generators are “definitely a viable option. A lot of homeowners like having propane for its clean burn and long storage life, with gasoline as a backup if they run through their propane supply.”

Westinghouse iGen4500 has a 3.4-gal. gas tank that can run quietly for up to 18 hours; has a variety of ports but weighs 100+ lbs. Read the review.

Propane generators use safer, easier to store, and cleaner-burning fuel than gasoline generators; gas generators are more affordable to purchase and operate, with better fuel efficiency. “For most homeowners looking for reliable backup power, propane is the better long-term solution. That said, if you’re looking for something more budget-friendly, gasoline can still get the job done,” says Goodrich.

After gaining a basic understanding of the pros and cons between propane vs. gasoline generators, it’s a good idea to start your search by reading up on the best generator brands, then researching individual products that offer the features you want. Keep in mind that at the end of the day, a dual-fuel generator, powered by propane and natural gas, will offer you the best of both worlds so you are prepared for any emergency.

The 7 Best LED Face Masks for Men in 2026, According to Experts

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

For battling blemishes and signs of aging, there are few better at-home tools.

AS SOMEONE RAISED on slasher horror movies, I was always going to gravitate towards LED face masks. But while their creepy Jason Voorhees-at-a-rave look is what initially grabbed my attention, the skincare benefits are what sold me on the products. LED face masks combine the firming power of anti-aging products, the depuffing of eye cream, the energizing boost of moisturizers, and the breakout-fighting strength of acne washes—making them one of the most versatile grooming tools out there.

LED masks use specific wavelengths of light to penetrate the skin and trigger cellular changes, according to dermatologist Dr. Hannah Kopelman, MD. This can include stimulating collagen production to reduce fine lines and support firmer skin, as well as treating acne-causing bacteria and calming inflammation to promote a clearer complexion. Some devices offer all of these benefits, while others are laser-focused (get it?) on just one or two. The key is to know what each is capable of and what service you’re looking for.

Dermatologist Dr. Brian Toy, MD, warns that the market is flooded with LED face masks that vary greatly in quality and effectiveness, so it’s best to start your search as informed as possible. To temper the confusion, I went ahead and used myself, along with fellow Men’s Health writers and editors, as guinea pigs. This way, you’ll know what works and what is merely an overpriced Halloween mask.

We gave Shark Beauty CryoGlow a 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award barely a month after it was released; that’s how great this LED mask is. It offers four separate treatment options that cover anything you could possibly want out of an LED face mask. The Better Aging setting uses red and infrared light to reduce wrinkles and firm skin, while Skin Clearing mode combines blue, red, and infrared light to fight blemishes and even tone.

The Skin Sustain maintains glow with a quick mix of all three LED wavelengths, and Under-Eye Revive uses cryotherapy-inspired cooling to depuff and tighten the under-eye area. You can also use this under-eye cooling ability combined with the other treatments, which roll out in three increasing levels of chill. Each is between four and eight minutes, meaning you don’t need to dedicate much time to combat whatever issue you’re after. Under-Eye Revive, you can do up to 15 minutes if you’d like, but you only need five to be effective.

Dr. Peterson Pierre, MD, FAAD, likes that this device uses red, blue, and infrared lights so that you can get a full smorgasbord of benefits, like combating acne, fighting signs of aging, reducing inflammation, and helping regulate oil production. He also digs the cooling feature and three levels of intensity. I’ve been using my CryoGlow for months, and have seen a noticeable change in the smoothness and clearness of my skin, as well as reduced redness, using The Better Aging and Skin Clearing settings. But where I saw the most immediate results was with eye puffiness.

If I’m ever running on limited sleep or recovering from a night out, I pop the mask on, and after a few minutes of Under-Eye Revive mode, I look like I’ve actually slept. The light from this device doesn’t feel glaring when you’re wearing it, so I was able to successfully walk around and multitask during my treatments.

Plus, as someone who is generally sensitive to light, it also feels a lot less intense than other options on this list, and never inspired headaches of any kind. Not to mention, it’s easy to adjust and fits my face perfectly. I only have a few nitpicks. Given the expansive options and customizability of this mask, there is a handheld controller attached to it to help you navigate. While this makes firing up the device super easy and you don’t need to rely on an app, the controller can be a bit awkward to deal with while you’re in treatment.

You can’t put it in your pocket without accidentally changing the setting, so you have to hold it, which limits the multitasking you’re able to do. Also, the mask is bulkier than its main competition for best overall, the Dr. Dennis Gross Face Mask. But when you consider that the CryoGlow is also the cheapest full-face option on this list, it’s a fair trade-off.

Read More: Shark CryoGlow LED Face Mask Review

Dr. Kopelman has been recommending this LED mask to patients for years. She likes that it is FDA-cleared and offers both red and blue light; however, what she likes most about it is that it consistently delivers results. In terms of effectiveness, it’s equal to the CryoGlow. The only reason it just missed out on the top spot is that it’s over $100 more expensive and offers fewer additional treatments, like under-eye cooling. Beyond that, I find it just as successful at battling blemishes and signs of aging as the Shark Beauty.

Plus, the treatments are shorter, and you only need to wear this for three minutes a day to see results. Unlike many other options, like the CurrentBody or FAQ 202, which are made of more flexible material you can mold to your face, this design is rigid. While that may seem like a drawback, I loved it. Of all the LED masks on this list, I found Dr. Dennis Gross to be the sturdiest, and it fit my face perfectly. It’s slim, without feeling flimsy, and doesn’t weigh down my face like other similarly sturdy masks that tend to be a bit heavier, such as the Theraface Mask.

That being said, I possess an incredibly average build and face shape, so if you fall outside of those parameters, the singular and unadaptable design of this mask might not be as perfect a fit. Unlike the CryoGlow, it’s wireless when you’re using it and can be conveniently charged with any USB-C charger. This helps when traveling, though the solid design poses some challenges if you’re tight on storage space.

Similar to the Dr. Dennis Gross mask, this device is crafted with a hard, contoured shell; however, it’s far less slim. But it trades off this added bulkiness with its vibrating ability, which soothes facial tension and boosts blood flow around the eyes, brows, and scalp. It offers red, blue, and infrared light therapy to target acne, improve skin tone, and increase collagen production.

You can choose between three- or nine-minute treatment modes, though we found the longer sessions to be more effective. Sure, this mask can feel a bit heavy or bulky on the face, but the results are legit. In fact, some effects can be seen immediately, and they only increase from there. “After the very first time I used it, my skin felt softer, and my pores looked smaller,” says Senior Gear and Commerce Editor Ryan Brower.

“Over time, my skin tone looks more even, and my skin appears to be firmer, smoother, and less puffy.” He adds that the massaging, vibrating feature is relaxing, although it can feel ticklish or even chill-inducing at times. Since it sits close to your ears, it can also get a bit loud, especially when multitasking. Still, it’s really easy to switch between settings, turn on and off, and choose the massage style you want.

If you’re solely looking to combat puffiness, dark circles, and wrinkles, Lumin is the way to go. Sure, it looks straight out of an abandoned Lone Ranger In Space reboot, but there is no device better at rejuvenating the skin around the eyes than this mask. One tester saw noticeable improvements after days of use with this device. “I naturally have darker circles, but after consistent daily use for about a week, I saw a noticeable difference in the brightness and overall alertness of my eye area,” she says. The mask stays in place well, and the soft silicone padding makes it comfortable throughout each session.

Its adjustable design also ensures it fits all face shapes and sizes with ease. The same tester also saw a brighter tone and smoother skin after a couple of weeks of daily use. “While I don’t personally have under-eye wrinkles, I can see how this would be especially helpful for someone who does or for anyone who spends a lot of time in the sun,” she says. Not to mention, the Luminator is quick and easy to use—just three minutes a day with an auto timer.

Our testers found that this FAQ mask makes a strong impression right out of the box with its ultra-thin, flexible design, which feels more like a high-end sheet mask than a tech device. You’ll need to download the app to get the most out of this tool, however. There’s a single button on the mask, but without the app, we found that it was nearly impossible to remember its function or how to power it off.

Once the app is set up and the mask is synced, navigating the features becomes straightforward—just select your desired treatment and that’s it. Despite being covered in tiny LED lights, the mask feels surprisingly lightweight and comfortable. During the 15-minute session, testers reported no heat or noticeable sensation on the skin and even forgot it was on while doing other tasks, such as reading. The mask stays comfortably in place, even when looking down at a book or phone.

We also appreciated the included cleaning spray. For anyone with sensitive or breakout-prone skin, keeping the mask clean is essential, and the spray makes that simple. After each use, we cleaned and dried the mask before placing it in its pouch, which securely holds the device and makes storage hassle-free. One minor concern was the split at the bridge of the nose—designed for flexibility—which left one tester wondering if that area was receiving full treatment. Still, this didn’t deter them from continuing to use it.

Women’s Health fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi says that the Qure Pro LED Mask has taken her nightly skincare regimen to the next level. After a month of use, she saw a dramatic difference in her skin’s appearance. She used to struggle with oily skin and frequent breakouts, but since regularly using the pink LED light setting, she says it has significantly reduced her sebum production. “I'm also approaching 30 (yikes), so I've been using the red LED light setting as well to help combat fine lines and reverse skin aging,” Accardi says.

Each session runs for three minutes and automatically shuts off when it’s done, so you never have to worry about timing it yourself. It’s perfect for anyone who wants results without the hassle. It’s one of the easiest, most low-maintenance skincare tools out there at a relatively low cost. That’s not to say $380 is cheap, but when it comes to legit, effective LED masks, you won’t find many other options under $400. It’s really just this and the CryoGlow.

If the more rigid masks, like CryoGlow, Qure, and Dr. Dennis Gross, are too bulky for you, but the FAQ is too small for your face, Currentbody will be your best option. This mask offers the most flexibility, with a silicone design that easily molds to the contours of any face, ensuring full coverage. This is as long as you tighten the straps. I’ve been lazy a few times with that, and it will start slipping off your face mid-treatment. In addition to the flexible fit, this mask feels super gentle on the face.

One of our testers used it only days after getting eye surgery with no issue. Didn’t bother her eyes one bit. That being said, it takes up to six hours for a full charge, which can be a bit annoying. This is the longest charge time on this list by a few hours, to be clear. I’m the type of person who pushes off charging a device until I absolutely have to, so this long charge time usually results in me skipping a day of treatment. But if you’re a better planner (to be fair, it’s a low bar compared to me), it’ll be less of an issue.

Depending on what skin issues or concerns you’re looking to address with your LED face mask, you’ll want to focus on which treatments it offers. This is driven by the color of light the device uses, which dictates its benefits. Some on this list offer multiple services, while others zero in on one. These are the common options:

While some are comfortable and allow for multitasking, there is no getting around the fact that you’re wearing a large light on your face. As a long-time migraine sufferer, having a light this close to my eyes for too long can be a trigger. But even if you’re perfectly fine with prolonged light exposure, you’ll want to know what the time commitment is before buying LED face masks, as they’re most effective when used regularly. Some are as long as 25 minutes, while others can be as short as three minutes. Keep in mind that not all are meant for everyday use; some (especially the ones with longer treatment lengths) may only need to be used a few times a week for max efficiency.

When shopping for an LED face mask, choosing a device that’s FDA-cleared is essential, says Dr. Kopelman. This ensures the product meets fundamental safety standards for consumer use. To be clear, however, FDA-cleared is not the same as FDA-approved—the latter involves extensive clinical trials and rigorous testing. Currently, no LED face masks on the market have achieved FDA approval.

For now, stick with FDA-cleared options, which means the device is proven to be as safe and effective as another legally marketed product. You might also see terms like FDA-registered or FDA-listed, but these simply indicate that the manufacturer has notified the FDA of the product's existence—there’s no review or evaluation involved. Because of that uncertainty, you won’t see any of those on this list.

There are a lot of LED face masks out there, and like any trendy tool, not all are created equal. So, before putting any to the test, I consulted with a panel of dermatologists on which devices were legit and which they recommend. They also advised me on what to look for in a quality LED face mask and the brands to focus on. Based on this intel, I, along with other Men’s Health writers and editors, put several masks to the test, evaluating each device’s effectiveness, ease of use, and how comfortable it was to wear.

As many LED face masks do not offer immediate results, we used each one for at least one month to ensure enough time was given to gain any possible benefits. Following this extensive research and testing, I landed on these seven LED face masks as the best for men in 2026.

The dermatologists I spoke to for this story were clear on this: you should be cleaning your device after every use. If you don’t, bacteria, oil, and product residue can build up on the surface and transfer back onto your skin, causing irritation or breakouts, which may ironically be what you were hoping to minimize by using an LED mask in the first place.

Dr. Kopelman says that LED masks should always be used on freshly cleansed, dry skin to ensure the light penetrates as effectively as possible. After the session, apply your serums and moisturizers—doing it beforehand can block the light and reduce its benefits. A hydrating serum like hyaluronic acid or a peptide-rich cream works especially well to complement the collagen boost from the treatment, Dr. Kopelman says.

According to Dr. Toy, be sure to skip any products that might react to light. For example, because retinol and vitamin C serums are photosensitizing, they’re an absolute no-go before any LED treatment. Dr. Chacon adds that reflective products like heavy oils or sunscreens should also be avoided during use as they can scatter the light and disrupt the device’s effectiveness.

16 Best Automatic Watches for Men 2026, According to GQ Watch Nerds

📅 Aug 29, 2025  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

A budding “watch guy” most likely starts off their collection with an assortment of quartz tickers (and let’s be clear, there’s nothing wrong with that). But as your interest in watches grows, it’s only natural for you to want something on your wrist you can brag about, which inevitably pushes you towards automatic watches.

Inside the case of an automatic watch is a weighted rotor that spins as you move your arm, a few little flicks of your wrist throughout the day keeps the internal mechanisms running long enough to keep that minute hand tick-tick-ticking across the dial.

But automatic watches also have a reputation for being finicky or costly. And while that can be true, the beauty of watches is the wide price scale in which the industry operates. From stunners for less than $250 to ones you’d have to mortgage your house (and maybe your parents’ house) to buy, here are the top automatic watches on the market today for any budget.

While not impossible to find a great watch at the $250-mark, you are going to be limited. Given the many internal pieces and complicated mechanisms needed to build an automatic watch, many brands have to charge a bit more for a quality automatic. Even so, brands like Orient and Seiko lead the way on well-made (and well-designed) options.

Orient’s range of inexpensive watches punch well above their weight-class and the Symphony III is no different. With its classic, clean design and movement that promises 40 hours of power reserve, this is a watch that’s made to be a daily driver without breaking the bank.

Timex’s Waterbury is a staple in their line-up and the extremely stylish Metrograph has an Art Deco-style case and dial that’s pared-down enough to keep things simple, but without looking boring.

The Seiko 5 is something of a cult favorite for the Japanese brand – and for good reason. It’s a perfect daily driver and a budget-friendly alternative to the Rolex Datejust. Best of all, it clocks in at just 37mm, which is the perfect case size for nearly any wrist.

As ever, Timex provides maximum bang for minimum buck with this classic "Pepsi" bezel diver.

At $500, the doorway starts to open up a bit more – but only a creak. The usual suspects like Timex and Casio, are populating this price point, Bulova and Sternglas are great alternatives who will give you a little more street cred among collectors.

Undoubtedly one of the best looking watches in the sub-$500 category, the Timex Marlin in this particular shade of green strikes the perfect balance between classic and modern.

Heavily influenced by motorsports, the Edifice is a bit of a departure from the digital, retro-charm of many mainstays for Casio. The integrated bracelet keeps it sporty, while the patterned dial makes it a little more interesting than other options on the market.

At 45mm, 200-meter of water resistance, and 42-hours of power reserve, the Bulova Marine Star ticks all the boxes for a great dive watch at a reasonable price – the two-toned bezel is just a nice bonus.

This fan favorite hits the bullseye of the style-quality-price nexus, and looks especially fetching with a bright yellow dial.

A thousand bucks is a perfectly reasonable budget to have when you want to upgrade your watch game without completely breaking the bank. Here, I’d recommend looking at smaller, or more indie brands to find some interesting designs not seen by more household names.

You’d be forgiven for not knowing their name, but Kuoe is starting to gain traction in the U.S.. The Japanese-based watchmaker produces high-quality, well-designed pieces that harken to a more classic watch style. The OLD SMITH is based on the military field watch, but with a slightly more refined design language.

A reborn grail from the Studio 54 era, with a vintage-correct 35mm case.

UNIMATIC uses the basic field watch as the springboard for their Modello Due, which strips it back to its barebones to make something a bit bolder, a bit more modern, and eye-catching.

Paulin is a Glasgow-based microbrand that’s known for colorful, unique, and whimsical watches, often playing with color to make their designs all the more interesting.

Needless to say, if money isn’t an issue, the sky’s the limit. Not all watches are created equal and buying just for the name recognition alone doesn’t always make for the best watch for the money. Instead, look for a price point that’s commensurate with the movement, design, and materials used, and you’ll never regret the decision to spend the big bucks.

Taken from a 1924 archival design, the Brunswick’s cushion case, clean lines, and mother-of-pearl dial may all feel a bit “precious”, shall we say; but this is a workhorse watch that’s destined to be a daily driver for anyone who is looking for a little eye-candy on the wrist.

The IWC Ingenieur is a masterfully made ceramic watch (and matching ceramic bracelet) that will no doubt get you a few compliments every time you wear it to the office.

Not many watches can be mistaken for a Bell & Ross watch with its larger proportions and signature square case shape. The BR-05, the brand’s most popular model, is a sportier, slightly bolder answer to Cartier’s Santos.

It’s hard to narrow down one Grand Seiko to choose, but the White Birch is subtle and versatile enough to dress up or use as your daily driver. Most impressive about this particular model is the Caliber 9SA5 movement, which promises a whopping 80-hours of power when fully wound – nearly twice that of many others on the market.

Mechanical watch movements fall into two basic categories: hand-wound and automatic. Before the invention of automatic wristwatches in the 1920s (and long before the invention of battery-powered quartz movements in the 1960s) all watches were hand-wound. That meant you needed to manually wind up your watch every day to keep it running. An automatic watch (also called a self-winding watch) doesn’t require this because it winds automatically with the movement of your body as you wear it.

Most automatic watches wind themselves via a weighted rotor, which you’ll be able to see if your watch has a see-through case back (it’s the half moon-shaped piece right on top). When you wear the watch and move around, the rotor winds a spring, which turns the hands, date wheel and everything else that moves on a watch.

To keep your watch from stopping when you’re sitting still (or when you take it off at night) automatic movements also store excess energy and slowly release it over hours or days while the rotor is stationary. This is called a “power reserve,” and it typically ranges from 40 to 80 hours, with some going as high as a week or more. They’re useful if you don’t wear a watch every day, and don’t want to have to reset the date and time every time you put it on—particularly with annual or perpetual calendar models that can be complicated to set.

It’s not a downside, per se, but they do require some upkeep. Unlike a quartz watch that requires nothing more than a new battery every few years, a mechanical watch is a finely-tuned machine consisting of many tiny, precisely calibrated parts. Watchmakers have made huge advances in shock-and waterproofing over the years, but there’s still only so much abuse a mechanical movement can take. And that’s the thing: repairs to automatic watches can be expensive.

If you stick to the manufacturer’s recommended service schedule (it’ll need an overhaul and lube every 4 to 10 years, depending on the brand and model) and don’t make a habit of wearing it in the sauna, you’ll probably be fine. Whether it’s a $200 Amazon special or a $200,000 grand complication, automatic watches are designed to be worn, so the best way to take care of your watch is to wear it as much as possible.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

8 Best Hotel Mattress Picks for a Five-Star Staycation (2026)
